subject: Arabic
source: Drive: Curriculum/Arabic folder and Secondary Lesson Plan - Arabic - Y8 (format and approach); Madinah-style progression (pronouns, nominal sentences); National Curriculum KS2 languages

lessons.title: I, you, he, she: personal pronouns
objectives: Use أَنَا، أَنْتَ، أَنْتِ، هُوَ، هِيَ correctly
Make nominal sentences such as أَنَا طَالِبٌ
starter: Say 'the book is on the table' in Arabic.
What do we call the little mark that doubles a sound?
Say 'my pen' and 'your pen' (to a boy) in Arabic.

teach.heading: Bismillah and pronouns
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and a short greeting dialogue (as-salaamu alaykum, kayfa haaluka). Explain that pronouns replace names so we do not repeat them. Elicit English pronouns first.

teach.heading: Four of the five
teach.note: Model each with gestures: point to self (ana), point to a boy picture (huwa), point to a girl picture (hiya). Choral drill. Common error: mixing huwa and hiya; use colour-coding.

teach.heading: You: boy and girl
teach.note: Arabic has two words for 'you'. The final vowel is the clue: fatha for a boy, kasra for a girl. Drill with a boy puppet and a girl puppet. Ask pupils to choose the right word for classmates.

teach.heading: Nominal sentences
teach.note: Arabic does not need 'am/is/are' in these sentences. Say ana taalib = 'I (am) a student'. Point out the female ending ة in taaliba/mu'allima. Pupils form sentences with a pronoun and a profession.

teach.heading: Practice with jobs
teach.note: Introduce طَبِيبٌ (doctor) and مُهَنْدِسٌ (engineer) as extension vocabulary. Show pictures. Pupils say a sentence about each picture using the right pronoun. Correct mismatches between pronoun and ending.

practice: Choose the correct pronoun for each picture of a boy and girl.
Say 'she is a teacher' and 'you (girl) are a student' in Arabic.
independent: Write six sentences using different pronouns and professions.
Match pictures of people to sentences.
Role-play a short dialogue with a partner.
exit: Say 'I am a student' in Arabic.
lessons.homework: Write five sentences about your family using هِيَ، هُوَ and أَنَا.
lessons.send: SEND: pronoun cards with picture clues, sentence frames. EAL: compare with home-language pronouns. Stretch: add the adjectives كَبِيرٌ/صَغِيرٌ to describe a person.

lessons.title: Introducing myself
objectives: Say name, nationality, religion and where you live in Arabic

keywords.def: where are you from? (to a boy)

starter: Say the five pronouns in Arabic.
Say 'she is a student' in Arabic.
What do we say to answer 'kayfa haaluk?'

teach.heading: Greeting and name
teach.note: Revise the greeting and name. Model a short self-introduction: as-salaamu alaykum, ismee Ahmad. Pupils replace Ahmad with their names. Ask: what comes next in an introduction?

teach.heading: Where are you from?
teach.note: Teach min = from and ayna = where. Pupils answer with their city or country. Provide city names in Arabic: لَنْدَن، مَانْشَسْتَر، بَرْمِنْغْهَام. Clarify the sound of the nasal 'ng' in birmingham in Arabic spelling.

teach.heading: Nationality and religion
teach.note: Boys use -iyy, girls use -iyya. Provide other nationalities: مِصْرِيٌّ (Egyptian), صُومَالِيٌّ (Somali), بَاكِسْتَانِيٌّ (Pakistani). Allow pupils to choose their own. Point out the shadda.

teach.heading: Where I live
teach.note: Introduce askunu = 'I live'. Pupils practise 'askunu fee ...'. Use maps to show city names. Reinforce the preposition fee.

teach.heading: Putting it together
teach.note: Model a four-line speech. Pupils produce their own. Encourage use of bismillah and polite phrases like tasharrafna. Record a short speech as a class.

practice: Say 'he is a teacher' in Arabic.
Ask your partner مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتَ؟ / مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتِ؟ and answer.
independent: Write a four-sentence introduction with greeting, name, nationality and where you live.
Interview a partner and record their answers in Arabic.
Draw a passport card for yourself with Arabic details.
exit: Say 'I live in London' in Arabic.
lessons.homework: Write and learn by heart a five-sentence introduction.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence strips and word bank. EAL: translate details from the home language. Stretch: add 'I like ...' to the introduction with أُحِبُّ.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Numbers and what I like
lessons.title: Numbers 1 to 10 and my age
objectives: Read the numbers in Arabic script
starter: Say 'I live in London' in Arabic.
Count from one to five in Arabic.

teach.heading: Numbers 1 to 5
teach.note: Revise numerals ١ ٢ ٣ ٤ ٥. Remind pupils that Arabic numerals look different but are used with the same value. Point out ٥ looks like a circle, and ٠ is a dot. Practise reading numerals from the board.

teach.heading: Numbers 6 to 10
teach.note: Introduce ٦ ٧ ٨ ٩ ١٠ with their words. Pupils write the numeral and word. Note ٧ looks like a V and ٨ looks like an inverted V. Use chanting and clapping.

teach.heading: More numbers
teach.note: Play 'count and clap': class counts to ten; clap on the even numbers. Then count backwards. Check for the difficult sound in thamaniya (th).

teach.heading: How old are you?
teach.note: Explain kam = how many, 'umr = age. Teach these ages as set phrases: سَبْعُ سَنَوَاتٍ، ثَمَانِي سَنَوَاتٍ، تِسْعُ سَنَوَاتٍ، عَشْرُ سَنَوَاتٍ. Do not explain the number-gender rule at this stage. Pupils say their own age.

teach.heading: Family ages
teach.note: Pupils use the pattern 'umru ... + family word to talk about relatives. Model with ukhtee. Practise in pairs. Offer a word bank for family members from earlier years.

practice: Count from one to five in Arabic.
Read the numerals aloud from ١ to ١٠.
Ask and answer كَمْ عُمْرُكَ؟ with a partner.
independent: Write the numerals and words for 1-10.
Write three sentences about the ages of family members.
exit: How do you say 'seven' in Arabic?
How do you ask 'How old are you?' in Arabic?
lessons.homework: Write your age and the ages of three family members in Arabic sentences.
lessons.send: SEND: number line with words and numerals. EAL: compare numeral shapes with home-language numerals. Stretch: say addition sums aloud in Arabic using وَ and يُسَاوِي.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Numbers and what I like
lessons.title: Food I like and do not like
objectives: Name ten foods and drinks in Arabic
Say what you like and do not like
starter: Count from six to ten in Arabic.

teach.heading: Food and drink
teach.note: Show pictures and say each word. Pupils echo. Use real examples from lunch or iftar. Ask: what do you usually drink in the morning?

teach.heading: More foods
teach.note: Dates are linked to the Sunnah of breaking the fast with dates. Pupils may know this; keep a gentle tone. Practise: say the word, then point to a picture.

teach.heading: I like
bullets: I like dates, I like juice
teach.note: Teach uhibbu + al- + noun. Note that the noun ending changes to -a after uhibbu (fatha). Model several. Pupils say what they like.

teach.heading: I do not like
teach.note: Teach laa to negate. Pupils choose something they do not like. Be sensitive: no need to criticise food. Encourage respectful language when someone dislikes something, and gratitude for food.

teach.heading: Eating with adab
teach.note: The Prophet ﷺ taught the boy 'Say Bismillah, eat with your right hand and eat from what is near you' (Sahih al-Bukhari and Muslim). Discuss manners with food. Pupils practise saying Bismillah and Alhamdulillah before and after eating.

practice: Say 'I am nine years old' in Arabic.
Count from one to ten in Arabic.
Say whether you like each food shown on the screen.
Ask a partner هَلْ تُحِبُّ ...؟ and answer with نَعَمْ or لَا.
independent: Write six sentences: three with أُحِبُّ, three with لَا أُحِبُّ.
Make a menu with five foods in Arabic.
Interview a partner and report one thing they like.
exit: How do you say 'I like dates' in Arabic?
What do we say before eating?
lessons.homework: Write a short paragraph about three foods you like and one you do not like.
lessons.send: SEND: picture menu with Arabic labels, sentence frames. EAL: share foods from home language and culture. Stretch: add 'because it is tasty' with لِأَنَّهُ لَذِيذٌ.
